item.research_question: How does temperature influence the deformation mechanisms, superplasticity, and strength-ductility trade-offs in CoNiCrFeMn high entropy alloy nanowires compared to single-component Ag nanowires?
item.material_system: CoNiCrFeMn equiatomic high entropy alloy (20 at.% each) and Silver (Ag) nanowires with circular (110) cross-section
item.processing_route: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS; nanowires extracted from bulk FCC crystals along [110] orientation; equilibrated at 77, 300, and 1000 K using Langevin thermostat and Berendsen barostat; constant strain rate of 10^8 1/s applied in NVT ensemble
item.test_conditions: Tensile deformation at cryogenic (77 K), room (300 K), and high (1000 K) temperatures with a strain rate of 10^8 1/s
key_findings: Ag nanowires exhibit superplasticity at 77 K via (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation driven by partial dislocation nucleation.
CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires reach a peak stress of approximately 6.2 GPa at 5–6% elongation at 77 K.
At 300 K, HEA nanowires achieve a stress of 5.5 GPa at around 5% strain with simultaneous activation of twinning and martensitic transformation.
At 1000 K, HEA nanowires maintain good flow stress and ductility, with the FCC-HCP martensitic transformation fraction being much higher than at lower temperatures.
Lomer Cottrell locks form in HEA nanowires at all temperatures, hindering dislocation motion and promoting work hardening.
The fraction of HCP phase in HEA nanowires increases rapidly at 1000 K due to the unlocking of Lomer Cottrell locks by stacking fault accumulation.
Dislocation density is highest at 77 K and decreases as temperature increases to 1000 K, shifting the dominant mechanism from TWIP to TRIP.
item.mechanism: The exceptional mechanical properties of HEA nanowires arise from a synergistic interaction of deformation twinning (TWIP), FCC-HCP martensitic transformation (TRIP), and cross-section reorientation. At low temperatures, Lomer Cottrell locks and stacking fault networks hinder dislocation motion, promoting work hardening and delaying necking. At high temperatures, thermal energy facilitates the unlocking of Lomer Cottrell locks via martensitic transformation, allowing the HCP phase to provide secondary reinforcement and enabling the TRIP effect.
item.limitations: The study relies on molecular dynamics simulations with specific interatomic potentials (EAM for Ag, 2NN MEAM for HEA) and a fixed strain rate of 10^8 1/s; the text notes that the calculated SFE values are estimations at 0 K.
item.future_work: The authors suggest these findings could be useful for designing nanowires at different temperatures with high stability and superior mechanical properties in the semiconductor industry.
quotes: HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.
Simultaneous activation of twining induced plasticity and transformation induced plasticity are responsible for the plasticity at different stages and temperatures.
The good refractory property of the HEA NW in this work is attributed to the same synergistic mechanism as the aforementioned one.
